title: Theorem Labs Launches OSS Verify for Crash Free Open Source Software
summary:
Software engineers can now use an automated system to certify that their code is immune to crashes or obtain the specific fixes needed to eliminate defects. The service, developed by Theorem Labs and called OSS Verify, is free for open-source projects and seeks to bootstrap a verified software ecosystem by scaling formal verification—a process that mathematically proves the absence of bugs—beyond its previous limitation to very small codebases.

The tool is based on research with Anthropic in which the Claude AI model verified 123 open-source libraries in a few weeks. During those tests, Claude wrote about 1 billion lines of formal proofs, with 180 million resulting in machine-checked proofs across 239 test entry points. The model also identified and patched hundreds of bugs, found a year's worth of security flaws in a PDF reader within a single week, and exposed mistakes in official x86 reference documentation.

Formal verification can prove that code is free of certain bugs, but historically it has only been feasible for small codebases (or required a lot of expert time).

selectedTweets.text:
This is INSANE. Anthropic says Claude wrote around one billion lines of formal proofs while trying to verify real-world software, with about 180 million lines ending up in machine-checked proofs covering 239 test entry points across 123 open-source libraries.

Along the way it found and patched hundreds of bugs. In separate experiments, Claude found in one week as many security bugs in a widely used PDF reader as are typically reported in a year, and autonomously generated x86 semantics that exposed hundreds of mistakes in official reference documentation plus some bugs in the hardware itself.

Anthropic is cooking. Fable 5.5 is going to be a beast.

selectedTweets.bestBit: spec: the binary never crashes on any input <= 64MB
selectedTweets.text:
tldr:
1. compile each project to a RISC-V binary
2. spec: the binary never crashes on any input <= 64MB
3. claude writes rocq proofs on top of theorem's risc-v + linux process semantics
4. if the proof checks, the fuzzer can never crash that binary
